name: Papuan Pidgin English
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 CLDF sources.bib (local copy) entries for papu1254: 45603 Mühlhäusler 1978 (Glottolog's most extensive description, grammar sketch;socling), 81003 Landtman 1927 (grammar sketch), 549220 Haddon 1907 (wordlist), 321446 Mühlhäusler & Dutton 1979 (socling), 585927 Avram 2020 (comparative)
sources.note: Bibliographic records only; our source list listed 0 Glottolog descriptive refs for this key, which is an indexing gap (the language has NOCODE language code and 5 refs).

sources.citation: Mühlhäusler, Peter. 1978. Papuan Pidgin English rediscovered. In S.A. Wurm & L. Carrington (eds), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: Proceedings, Fascicle 2. Pacific Linguistics C-61: 1377-1446. Canberra: ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C61.1377
sources.note: Grammatical sketch (§8) with a '(i) Pronunciation' subsection, pp. 1403-1405: vowel epenthesis, reduction to bisyllabic words, cluster reduction, reduced consonant inventory, five vowels + four diphthongs; rising intonation in yes/no questions (p. 1415). Nothing at all on word stress or accent; note 12 (p. 1433): 'I have not as yet carried out a phonological analysis of my data'.

sources.citation: Avram, Andrei A. 2020. Some notes on Papuan Pidgin English. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 38: 124-147.
sources.note: Diagnostic-feature (Baker & Huber 2001) and lexical comparison with Tok Pisin; no phonology section. p. 126: earlyetymological spelling 'which makes it difficult to reconstruct in detail the phonology of the language'. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Papuan Pidgin English' (stub, cites Smith 1994 annotated list)
sources.note: Nothing; era 1880-1925, replaced by Hiri Motu, not ancestral to Tok Pisin.

sources.citation: Landtman, Gunnar. 1918. The Pidgin-English of British New Guinea. Neuphilologische Mitteilungen 19(3/4): 62-74.
sources.note: Grammar sketch of Kiwai Pidgin-English plus a text. Pronunciation remark p. 65 only (varies by country; Kiwai have little difficulty except j, ch, th). The only prosodic remark, pp. 67-68, concerns expressive narrative emphasis: 'the emphasizing of certain parts of the speech, generally the last syllable of one of the leading words.. he go-gogo-go-ooo!' with a 'protracted singing or howling sound' — expressive lengthening, not a word-stress rule. No statement of word stress.

sources.citation: Haddon, A.C. [data] in Sidney H. Ray (ed.). 1907. The Jargon English of Torres Straits. Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, Vol. III: Linguistics, 251-254. Cambridge: CUP.
sources.note: Grammar notes and phrase vocabulary of the Torres Straits jargon, stated to be used also 'by the people of Mowata and Kiwai on the opposite coast of New Guinea'. Nothing on pronunciation or stress (only 'Exclamations. Emphasis: by golly!').

sources.citation: Baker, Philip & Peter Mühlhäusler. 1996. The origins and diffusion of Pidgin English in the Pacific. In Wurm, Mühlhäusler & Tryon (eds), Atlas of Languages of Intercultural Communication in the Pacific, Asia, and the Americas, vol. II.1, 551-594. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
